intro: Martial arts can be sorted into families: grappling, striking, armed as sport, flowing practice, diaspora and modern mix. Real bodies have drawn such lists, from the Japanese Budo Association in 1977 to UNESCO's heritage list. In this unit you will read those lists as records made by people, in given years, for their own purposes.

You will meet arts from Iceland, France, Japan, China, Trinidad, Israel and Switzerland. Glima went to the 1912 Stockholm Olympics as a demonstration. Kalinda survived a colonial law in 1884. Aikido chose to hold no contests, while fencing has been at every modern Olympic Games.

In the second chapter you will compare two sword sports, fencing and kendo, by origin, room, nation and code. You will use dated charters, federation records and rule books. By the end, you can build a comparison that explains differences with evidence and does not rank one art above another.
bigQuestion: How can a historian compare martial arts from different places fairly, using dated records instead of ranking them?

title: Compare Without Ranking

chapters.title: Six Rooms Again
chapters.bigQuestion: How can sorting martial arts into families help a historian compare them without claiming that one is better?

story.title: Six Objects on a Shelf
story.kicker: Each object on the shelf points to a different room and a different set of records.
paragraphs: A museum storage shelf holds six objects with paper tags. There is a leather belt harness from Iceland and a pair of laced French boxing shoes. There is a bamboo practice sword from Japan and a printed booklet of a simplified taijiquan routine from Beijing, dated 1956.

The last two objects are a polished stick from Trinidad and a training manual in Hebrew from Israel. A curator must file them. One tag asks for a family name: grappling, striking, armed as sport, flowing practice, diaspora, or modern mix.

The curator notices that the tags do not rank the objects. A grappling harness is not higher than a stick. Each category only groups things that share a trait, such as a weapon, a contest, or a history of travel. Some objects could fit under two tags at once.

Scholars of martial arts face the same filing problem. Japanese federations, American authors and UNESCO have each drawn up lists and families. Every list was made by a real body, in a real year, for its own purpose. Reading who made a list is the first step in using it well.
story.think: Why might one object fit under two tags, and what does that tell you about categories?

lessons.title: Nine Arts, One Association
lessons.mainIdea: The Japanese Budo Association, founded in 1977, groups nine modern budo arts, so its list is a record of one body's choices.
reading: In 1977 nine Japanese federations joined with the Nippon Budokan to form the *Japanese Budo Association*. The nine arts were judo, kendo, kyudo, sumo, karatedo, aikido, shorinji kempo, naginata and jukendo. Kyudo is Japanese archery. Naginata uses a long curved blade on a pole, and jukendo uses a wooden rifle with a blunt bayonet.

The Nippon Budokan is the hall in Tokyo built for judo at the 1964 Olympic Games. It became the home of the new association. In 1987 the association issued the *Budo Charter*, a short document of principles. The charter describes budo as a way of building character, respect and self-discipline, in the words of its authors.

The list is a *category*, a group drawn around shared traits. Its borders were set by people. Many Japanese arts older than 1868 are not on it, and neither is kickboxing. The list tells a historian which modern federations worked together in Japan after 1977. It does not say those nine arts are better than others.

words.d: a body formed in 1977 by nine Japanese budo federations and the Nippon Budokan
a 1987 statement of principles for modern budo issued by the Japanese Budo Association
a group that people draw around things sharing a trait
a modern Japanese budo art practiced with a wooden rifle and bayonet

lessons.title: Old Schools and New Budo
lessons.mainIdea: Japanese historians often separate koryu, schools founded before 1868, from gendai budo, arts shaped in modern Japan, but the line is a tool.
reading: In Japan the word *koryu* means old school or old stream. It usually names a martial tradition founded before the Meiji Restoration of 1868. Many koryu passed teaching through one family or one licensed line. They kept written scrolls that listed the school's founder and its later heads.

The word *gendai budo* means modern budo. It names arts organized after 1868, such as judo from 1882, kendo's national rules, aikido and karatedo. Gendai budo usually has open membership, printed rules and national federations. Many of these arts also hold public contests with referees.

The American author Donn F. Draeger wrote three books on this split: *Classical Bujutsu* and *Classical Budo* in 1973 and *Modern Bujutsu and Budo* in 1974. He used 1868 as a working border. Later historians noted that many koryu kept changing after 1868 and that modern arts borrowed from old ones. The border helps sort records; it does not settle which art is more genuine.

words.d: a Japanese martial tradition, usually one founded before 1868; literally old school or old stream
modern budo; Japanese arts organized after 1868 with open membership and printed rules
the 1868 change that returned rule to the Japanese emperor and began rapid modernization

look.title: A Working Border in Three Books
look.text: Draeger divided Japanese fighting arts by period. Classical arts came from the age of the warrior class before 1868. Modern arts grew after 1868, when Japan built schools, an army of conscripts and national sport bodies.

check.why: Koryu means old school or old stream and usually names a tradition founded before 1868.

check.why: Historians noted change after 1868 and borrowing between old and new arts.

lessons.title: A Heritage List as a Map
lessons.mainIdea: UNESCO's list of intangible cultural heritage has named several martial practices since 2010, each nominated by a state for its own reasons.
reading: UNESCO adopted a Convention for the Safeguarding of the *Intangible Cultural Heritage* in 2003. Intangible heritage means living practices such as songs, crafts, festivals and games, not buildings. A state nominates a practice, and a UNESCO committee decides whether to inscribe it on a list.

Turkey's Kırkpınar oil wrestling festival and Iran's Pahlevani and zoorkhanei rituals were inscribed in 2010. South Korea's taekkyeon followed in 2011, Brazil's capoeira circle in 2014, and Korean ssireum in 2018. That ssireum listing was the first joint nomination by North and South Korea. Taijiquan from China joined in 2020.

The list mixes wrestling, ritual exercise, music and flowing routines. What joins them is a *nomination*, a formal request by a government. Governments choose what to nominate for reasons of pride, tourism and protection. A historian reads the list as a record of states naming their heritage, not as a ranking of arts.

words.d: living practices such as songs, games and rituals that UNESCO lists for protection
a formal request by a state asking UNESCO to list a practice
Korean wrestling, listed by UNESCO in 2018 after a joint nomination by both Koreas

lessons.title: Glima in Stockholm
lessons.mainIdea: Icelandic glima, a belt wrestling tradition, was shown to the world as a demonstration at the 1912 Stockholm Olympics.
reading: *Glima* is the traditional wrestling of Iceland. Wrestlers wear a leather belt harness around the waist and thighs, and they hold it during a bout. Icelandic sagas written down in the 1200s and 1300s describe men wrestling at gatherings. Glima is often named as Iceland's national sport.

At the 1912 Olympic Games in Stockholm, Icelandic wrestlers performed glima as a *demonstration*. A demonstration event is shown at the Games but awards no official Olympic medals. Iceland was then still under the Danish crown. Showing glima in Stockholm let Icelanders present a sport of their own to a world audience.

Glima belongs to the grappling family, the arts where contestants seize and control each other rather than strike. The family is very old and very wide. It also holds Greek wrestling, Japanese sumo, Mongolian bökh and Swiss schwingen. Each kept its own clothing, ring and rules, so the family name groups them without merging them.

words.d: the traditional belt wrestling of Iceland
an event shown at the Olympic Games that awards no official medals
a family of arts in which contestants seize and control each other rather than strike

lessons.title: Savate in Paris
lessons.mainIdea: Savate, or boxe française, grew in Paris in the 1800s when French teachers joined foot fighting with English boxing into a rule-bound sport.
reading: In the early 1800s, *savate* was a street fighting style in Paris and the port of Marseille. Its name comes from an old French word for a worn shoe. Michel Casseux, a Paris teacher, opened a training room for it in the 1820s. Police and polite society often saw savate as the fighting of the poor.

Charles Lecour, a pupil of Casseux, studied English boxing in the 1830s. He joined English punching with French kicking and taught the blend in his salle, or training hall. The result came to be called *boxe française*, French boxing. Wealthy Parisians began to attend Lecour's salle.

Late in the century, Joseph Charlemont and his son Charles ran a well-known Paris salle and wrote books on the sport. Their work gave boxe française printed rules and a teaching system. Savate belongs to the striking family, which also holds boxing, Muay Thai and karate. Like those arts, it moved from street or village use to a salle with rules.

words.d: a French fighting sport with kicks and punches; also called boxe française
French boxing; the name for savate after teachers blended it with English boxing
French for hall; a training room for fencing or French boxing
a family of arts in which contestants score with blows, such as boxing and karate

look.prompt: How did moving savate into a paid salle change who practiced it and how others saw it?

lessons.title: Kickboxing Gets a Name
lessons.mainIdea: The word kickboxing was coined in Japan in the mid-1960s for a new ring sport drawn from Muay Thai, karate and boxing.
reading: In the early 1960s, Thai boxers and Japanese karate fighters met in bouts in Japan and Thailand. The Japanese promoter Noguchi Osamu watched these meetings. In the mid-1960s he organized a new ring sport and gave it the English name *kickboxing*. Japanese television soon broadcast kickboxing cards, and the sport grew popular in Japan.

Kickboxing was a *hybrid*, a sport built from parts of several older arts. It kept the gloves and rounds of Western boxing. It borrowed scoring and kicks from Muay Thai and fighters from karate schools. Its rule books were new, and so were its title belts and weight classes.

In 1993 a Japanese karate leader, Ishii Kazuyoshi, founded the K-1 promotion in Japan. K-1 held kickboxing tournaments with fighters from many countries. Kickboxing shows how a modern mix grows: promoters, broadcasters and rule writers join pieces of older arts into a new *promotion*. The sport's history can be read in its founding years and its companies.

words.d: a ring sport named in Japan in the 1960s that joins boxing gloves and rounds with kicks
something built by joining parts of several older things
a company that organizes and sells public fight events

check.why: The promoter Noguchi Osamu organized and named kickboxing in the mid-1960s.

lessons.title: Bamboo and Armor
lessons.mainIdea: In the 1700s, Japanese sword schools adopted bamboo swords and padded armor, which later let kendo become a contest sport.
reading: Early Japanese sword schools trained mostly with wooden swords in set, paired routines. In the 1700s, teachers in the Jikishinkage-ryū and Ittō-ryū lines are credited with spreading protective armor and bamboo swords. The *shinai* is a practice sword made of four bamboo staves bound with leather. The armor, called *bogu*, covers the head, body and hands.

The new gear allowed full-speed contests with less risk of injury. By the early 1800s, large sword training halls in Edo, today's Tokyo, held such contests. After 1868 the sword lost its place in daily life, and the contests became public shows called gekiken. Around 1920 the Dai Nippon Butoku Kai adopted the name kendo, the way of the sword.

Kendo belongs to the armed-as-sport family. In these arts, a weapon has been made safe enough to score with. Olympic fencing, sport arnis and kendo all share this trait. In each, a change in equipment came before a change in rules, and the rules then shaped how the sport was judged.

words.d: a kendo practice sword made of four bamboo staves bound with leather
kendo armor covering the head, body and hands
a family of arts in which a weapon has been made safe enough to score with in contests

look.title: Wood, Then Bamboo

look.prompt: Why would the bamboo sword and helmet make scored contests possible where the oak sword did not?

check.q: What is a shinai made of?

check.why: A shinai is four bamboo staves bound with leather.

check.q: When did the Dai Nippon Butoku Kai adopt the name kendo?
check.why: The Butoku Kai adopted the name kendo around 1920.

check.why: Arts in this family made a weapon safe enough for scored contests.

lessons.title: Taijiquan in a Beijing Park
lessons.mainIdea: Taijiquan spread from Chen Village to Beijing in the 1800s, and a 1956 simplified routine made it a mass health practice in China.
reading: Yang Luchan, who lived from 1799 to 1872, studied taijiquan with the Chen family in Henan Province. He later taught in Beijing, the capital of the Qing dynasty. His students included men of the Manchu banner households. The Yang family line he began became one of the most practiced forms of taijiquan in the world.

In 1956 China's national sports commission published a *simplified* taijiquan routine of 24 movements. It was drawn from Yang-style forms and was shorter than older family routines. The goal was a practice that millions of people could learn for health. Group practice in parks and squares at dawn became a familiar sight in Chinese cities.

Taijiquan is often placed in a flowing family: *solo forms* done slowly, often without a partner or opponent. Many practitioners describe it as exercise, health care and moving meditation. Contest events also exist, such as judged taijiquan routines in modern wushu. So the same art can be sorted into more than one family, depending on the room.

words.d: made shorter and easier; the 1956 taijiquan routine had 24 movements
a set routine practiced by one person, without a partner
a teacher (1799–1872) who learned taijiquan in Chen Village and taught it in Beijing

look.title: Dawn in a Square
look.text: Six in the morning in a Beijing park. Forty retired workers move slowly in rows while a small speaker plays music. A leader faces them. Nobody keeps score. Nearby, a printed poster names the 24-movement routine and the year 1956.
look.prompt: Which family would you file this scene under, and what could make you file the same art somewhere else?

check.why: Yang Luchan taught in Beijing, the Qing capital.

check.q: How many movements did the 1956 simplified routine have?
check.why: The 1956 routine from China's sports commission had 24 movements.

check.q: Why can taijiquan fit more than one family?

lessons.title: Aikido Without Contests
lessons.mainIdea: Ueshiba Morihei's aikido, named in 1942, was organized by the Aikikai largely without competitions, while a later branch added them.
reading: Ueshiba Morihei, who lived from 1883 to 1969, studied Daitō-ryū jujutsu under Takeda Sōkaku from 1915. In 1931 he opened a training hall in Tokyo called the Kobukan. The name *aikido* came into official use in 1942. After the war, in 1948, Japan's government approved the *Aikikai* as a foundation to run the art.

The Aikikai chose not to hold contests. Its members practice in pairs and test for ranks before examiners instead of winners and losers. Ueshiba described aikido in spiritual and ethical terms, as a way of harmony. Those are his words and beliefs, and many Aikikai schools teach them as part of the art.

Not every aikido teacher agreed. Tomiki Kenji, a judo and aikido teacher, developed an aikido branch that includes competition. So aikido itself has more than one room. A family label such as flowing practice fits one branch well and the other less well.

words.d: a Japanese art founded by Ueshiba Morihei; the name came into official use in 1942
the foundation approved in 1948 to run Ueshiba's aikido, which holds no contests
a legally recognized body set up to carry on a purpose, such as teaching an art

check.why: Ueshiba studied Daitō-ryū jujutsu under Takeda Sōkaku from 1915.

lessons.title: Kalinda in Trinidad
lessons.mainIdea: Kalinda stick fighting in Trinidad grew among Africans and their descendants, and colonial laws in the 1880s tried to restrict it.
reading: *Kalinda* is a stick-fighting tradition of Trinidad in the Caribbean. It grew among enslaved Africans and their descendants on the island. Fighters, called *batonniers*, meet in a ring while drummers and singers perform. The songs, called kalinda songs, are part of the event, not an extra.

Britain ended slavery in its colonies by law in 1834, with full freedom in 1838. Freed people in Trinidad made Carnival their own, including the night festival of Canboulay. In 1881 police in Port of Spain tried to stop the Canboulay procession, and fighting broke out. In 1884 the colonial government passed a law that restricted drumming and the gatherings of stick-fighting bands.

Kalinda survived in villages and at Carnival. Trinidad and Tobago became independent in 1962, and stick-fighting contests still appear in its Carnival season. Kalinda belongs to the *diaspora* family: arts carried or rebuilt by people scattered from a homeland. Afro-Brazilian capoeira, with its music and ring, shows a similar history of law and survival.

words.d: an Afro-Trinidadian stick-fighting tradition with drumming and song
a stick fighter in Trinidad's kalinda tradition
people scattered from a homeland, and the culture they carry or rebuild
a night Carnival procession in Trinidad; police tried to stop it in 1881

look.text: Brazil, 1890: a penal code names capoeira a crime. Trinidad, 1884: a colonial law restricts drumming and stick-fighting bands. Both arts were practiced by people of African descent. Both came with music. Both survived and are now shown as national heritage.
look.prompt: What does the pattern in these two laws suggest about why governments targeted these arts?

lessons.title: Krav Maga in Israel
lessons.mainIdea: Imi Lichtenfeld built krav maga, a modern mixed self-defense system, for Jewish defense groups and then the Israel Defense Forces.
reading: Imi Lichtenfeld, who lived from 1910 to 1998, grew up in Bratislava, then in Czechoslovakia. He competed in boxing, wrestling and gymnastics. In the 1930s he helped organize Jewish young people to defend their neighborhoods against antisemitic gangs. He left Europe in 1940 and reached Mandatory Palestine, then under British rule, in the early 1940s.

There he trained fighters of the Haganah, a Jewish defense force. After Israel became a state in 1948, he became chief instructor of physical fitness and *krav maga* for the Israel Defense Forces. The Hebrew name means contact combat. He retired from the army in 1964 and then opened civilian schools.

Krav maga is a *modern mix*: a system built in the twentieth century from boxing, wrestling and other sources, with no contest code. Its main room was a military one, not a stadium. Sambo in the Soviet Union and kickboxing in Japan are other modern mixes. Each was shaped by a specific institution, in a specific decade, for a specific purpose.

words.d: a self-defense system built by Imi Lichtenfeld; the Hebrew name means contact combat
a system built in modern times from several older arts
a Jewish defense force in Mandatory Palestine before Israel became a state in 1948

look.title: Three Modern Mixes, Three Owners
look.text: Kickboxing: a Japanese promoter and television, 1960s. Sambo: Soviet sports and army bodies, 1930s. Krav maga: the Israel Defense Forces, after 1948. Each borrowed from older arts. Each served the body that shaped it.
look.prompt: How did the institution behind each mix shape whether it kept a contest code?

check.q: What does krav maga mean in Hebrew?
check.why: Krav maga means contact combat in Hebrew.

check.q: Which institution was krav maga's main room after 1948?
check.why: Lichtenfeld was chief instructor of krav maga for the Israel Defense Forces.

check.q: Where did Imi Lichtenfeld grow up?
check.why: Lichtenfeld grew up in Bratislava, then in Czechoslovakia.

chapters.title: Capstone Compare
chapters.bigQuestion: How can two sword sports, Olympic fencing and kendo, be compared by origin, room, nation and code using dated records?

story.title: Two Rule Books, One Page Each
story.kicker: Two rule books open to the page that says who may step forward and begin.
paragraphs: On a library table lie two rule books. One is the rule book of the International Fencing Federation, known by its French initials, FIE. The other is a set of kendo match regulations from the International Kendo Federation. A student has opened each to the page that names who may compete.

The fencing page says a fencer must hold a licence from the FIE, issued through a national federation. It also lists the commands a referee gives in French to begin a bout. The kendo page describes three referees, each holding a red flag and a white flag, and the command that starts a match.

Both sports use a blade that cannot cut. Both began in rooms where people once trained for real sword fights. Yet one became part of every modern Olympic Games, and the other has never been on the Olympic program.

A fair comparison sets these facts side by side with their dates. It asks where each sport began, what rooms it used, which nations shaped it, and which bodies wrote its code. It does not ask which sword sport is better.
story.think: What can the first page of a rule book tell you about the body that wrote it?

lessons.title: Masters of Arms in Paris
lessons.mainIdea: Fencing masters in Paris received a royal charter in 1567, and their salles turned sword training into a taught, regulated craft.
reading: In 1567 King Charles IX of France granted letters patent to the fencing masters of Paris. *Letters patent* are an open royal document that grants a right or a status. The charter let the masters govern their own trade, test new teachers and control who could teach. A master of arms had to pass through years as a pupil and assistant.

Training took place in a *salle d'armes*, a hall of arms. In the 1600s and 1700s, gentlemen carried a light thrusting sword called the smallsword. French masters developed a lighter training weapon, the foil, with a blunted tip. They also wrote conventions about which fencer had the right to score first.

Those conventions later became the rules of foil fencing. The salle was both a school and a social club for men of the upper classes. Women and working people were mostly shut out of it for centuries. The French words used in the salle, such as en garde, stayed in fencing everywhere.

words.d: an open royal document granting a right or status, such as the 1567 charter to Paris fencing masters
a hall of arms; a fencing school
a light fencing weapon with a blunted tip, first made for training

look.prompt: How did the 1567 charter decide who could teach fencing, and whom might it leave out?

check.why: King Charles IX granted letters patent to the Paris masters in 1567.

choices: A fencing school or hall of arms

check.why: French masters developed the blunted foil as a light training weapon.

lessons.title: Sword Halls in Edo
lessons.mainIdea: In the 1800s, large sword halls in Edo taught thousands of students with bamboo swords, creating the rooms that later became kendo.
reading: Edo, now Tokyo, was the seat of the Tokugawa shoguns from 1603 to 1868. By the early 1800s the city had many sword *dojo*, training halls tied to a named school. Three became famous as the great halls of Edo. They belonged to the Hokushin Ittō-ryū, the Shintō Munen-ryū and the Kyōshin Meichi-ryū.

Chiba Shūsaku founded the Hokushin Ittō-ryū and opened his Genbukan hall in Edo in the 1820s. His hall trained with shinai and armor and drew many students. Students were mostly from samurai families, though some commoners also trained. Young men from many domains came to the capital to study at these halls.

A dojo of this kind had a named *school*, or ryū, a founder, and licenses that recorded a student's progress. That makes it similar to the Paris salle, with its guild and masters. Both were private teaching rooms, and both ruled who could teach. Neither was yet a national sport body.

words.d: a training hall; in the Edo period, one tied to a named sword school
a Japanese school or tradition of an art, with a founder and a line of teachers
the old name of Tokyo, seat of the Tokugawa shoguns from 1603 to 1868

look.text: Paris salle, 1700s: a master licensed by a guild, pupils from the upper classes, a blunted foil. Edo dojo, 1820s: a founder of a named school, pupils mostly from samurai families, a bamboo shinai. Each room keeps its own records of who may teach.
look.prompt: Name two ways these rooms were alike and one way they differed.

check.why: Edo was the old name of Tokyo, the Tokugawa capital.

lessons.title: When Swords Left Daily Life
lessons.mainIdea: Japan banned wearing swords in public in 1876, while France allowed dueling far longer, and both changes pushed sword arts toward sport.
reading: In 1876 the Meiji government issued the *Haitōrei*, an order that banned most people from wearing swords in public. The samurai class had already lost its legal privileges. Sword teachers lost pupils and income. Some staged public gekiken shows with paid tickets to earn a living.

In France, the sword stayed in public life longer through the *duel*, a private fight arranged to settle a question of honor. Duels were illegal in theory but often tolerated. The épée, a heavier thrusting sword used in duels, became a sport weapon in the late 1800s. The last widely reported duel in France took place in 1967, between two politicians, Gaston Defferre and René Ribière.

In both countries the real sword faded from daily life over the same broad period. Sword training then needed a new reason to exist. In Japan the new reason was national education and budo. In France it was sport, clubs and international contests, including the Olympic Games from 1896.

words.d: the 1876 Japanese order that banned most people from wearing swords in public
a private fight arranged to settle a question of honor
a heavier fencing sword based on the dueling sword

lessons.title: The FIE, Paris 1913
lessons.mainIdea: The International Fencing Federation was founded in Paris in 1913, and French remains the language of fencing's commands.
reading: Fencing was on the program of the first modern Olympic Games at Athens in 1896. It is one of only a few sports held at every modern Games. At first each country and each tournament used its own rules. Disputes over judging were common, because a touch was hard to see and judges often disagreed.

In 1913 national federations met in Paris and founded the *Fédération Internationale d'Escrime*, the FIE. An *international federation* is a body that writes one set of rules for a sport across countries. The FIE took over the rules for foil, épée and sabre. Today its headquarters are in Lausanne, Switzerland, the city that also hosts the International Olympic Committee.

The FIE rules give referee commands in French. A referee says en garde, then prêts, then allez to begin, and halte to stop. A fencer in Tokyo or Chicago hears the same French words. Language in a rule book keeps a record of where a sport's code was first written.

words.d: Fédération Internationale d'Escrime; the International Fencing Federation, founded in Paris in 1913
a body that writes one set of rules for a sport across many countries
the French command a fencing referee gives to set fencers ready

check.why: National federations founded the FIE in Paris in 1913.

check.why: FIE rules give referee commands in French, such as en garde and allez.

check.q: What does an international federation do?
choices: Writes one set of rules for a sport across countries
check.why: An international federation writes common rules across many countries.

lessons.title: Kendo Federations, 1952 and 1970
lessons.mainIdea: Kendo gained a national federation in 1952 and an international one in 1970, which held the first World Kendo Championships that year.
reading: The All Japan Kendo Federation was founded in 1952, after the Allied occupation of Japan ended. It wrote national rules and ran grading examinations. In the United States, Japanese American clubs had practiced kendo since before the Second World War. Clubs also grew in Brazil, Korea, Taiwan and Europe.

In 1970 national and regional kendo federations founded the International Kendo Federation, known as the *FIK*. That same year the FIK held the first World Kendo Championships in Tokyo. The world championships have been held every three years since then, in cities from São Paulo to Paris.

Kendo is not an Olympic sport. Many kendo leaders have argued that Olympic entry would push the art toward winning and away from its educational aims. That argument is a choice about the room kendo wants. Fencing made the opposite choice in 1896 and stayed with it.

words.d: the International Kendo Federation, founded in 1970
international kendo contests held every three years since 1970
the national body for kendo in Japan, founded in 1952

look.title: Two Answers to One Invitation
look.text: Fencing, 1896: on the program in Athens and never left. Kendo, 1970 onward: world championships every three years, but no Olympic event. Both have world bodies, rule books and ranked referees.
look.prompt: Why might two sports with world federations make different choices about the Olympic Games?

check.why: The All Japan Kendo Federation was founded in 1952.

check.q: Where were the first World Kendo Championships held?
check.why: The FIK held the first World Kendo Championships in Tokyo in 1970.

check.q: What reason have many kendo leaders given for staying out of the Olympics?
choices: It could push the art toward winning and away from education
check.why: Many kendo leaders argue Olympic entry would shift kendo toward winning over its educational aims.

lessons.title: Wire Versus Flags
lessons.mainIdea: Fencing adopted electric scoring for épée at the 1936 Olympics, while kendo still relies on three referees with flags.
reading: At the 1936 Olympic Games in Berlin, épée bouts were scored with *electric scoring* for the first time. A wire connected each fencer's weapon to a box that lit a lamp when a touch landed. Foil followed at the 1956 Games in Melbourne. Sabre was the last weapon to go electric, in the late 1980s.

Kendo took a different path. A kendo match has three *shinpan*, or referees, each holding a red flag and a white flag. A point, called ippon, counts when at least two referees raise their flags for the same competitor. The referees judge not only contact but also form, spirit and posture, following the federation's rules.

The two systems record different ideas of what a point is. Fencing's machine answers whether a touch landed, and a referee applies the right-of-way conventions in foil and sabre. Kendo's panel asks whether a strike met the federation's full standard. Neither system is more modern in a ranking sense; each fits its own code.

words.d: a system in which a wired weapon lights a lamp when a touch lands; first used for Olympic épée in 1936
a kendo referee; a match has three, each with a red and a white flag
in kendo, a point awarded when at least two of three referees raise their flags

look.prompt: What does each scene show about who or what decides a point?

check.why: Épée used electric scoring at the 1936 Berlin Games.

check.why: A kendo match has three referees, each with a red and a white flag.

choices: When at least two referees raise flags for the same side
check.why: Ippon counts when at least two of three shinpan raise flags for one competitor.

lessons.title: A Licence to Enter
lessons.mainIdea: To enter FIE competitions, a fencer must hold an FIE licence issued through a national federation, a paper gate that ties each fencer to a nation.
reading: The FIE requires every fencer in its official events to hold an FIE *licence*. A licence is a paper or digital permit that shows a person may take part. Fencers get it through their national federation, which the FIE recognizes. Without one, a fencer cannot start in a World Cup or world championship bout.

This rule ties each fencer to a nation. In the United States, the national body began as the Amateur Fencers League of America in 1891. It is now called USA Fencing. National bodies choose teams, and those teams represent their countries at the Olympic Games.

The licence gives the FIE a list of who fenced, where and for which nation. That list is a historian's record. It shows when new countries joined, when fencers changed nations, and when events opened. It also shows the gate: only those accepted by a national body may begin.

words.d: a permit showing that a person may take part; FIE events require one
the body that runs a sport in one country and is recognized by the world body
the national fencing body of the United States, founded in 1891 as the Amateur Fencers League of America

look.text: A fencer from Chicago wins a regional tournament and wants to enter a World Cup event abroad. The entry form asks for an FIE licence number. She must first be registered with USA Fencing and entered by it.
look.prompt: What steps stand between a strong local fencer and a world event, and who controls each step?

check.why: The FIE requires a licence for every fencer in its official events.

check.q: Through which body does a fencer get an FIE licence?
check.why: Fencers get the licence through their national federation.

check.q: What was USA Fencing called when it was founded in 1891?
choices: The Amateur Fencers League of America
check.why: USA Fencing began as the Amateur Fencers League of America in 1891.

lessons.title: A Grade Exam to Rise
lessons.mainIdea: In kendo, the national federation ranks practitioners through dan examinations up to eighth dan, which very few candidates pass in any year.
reading: The All Japan Kendo Federation runs *dan* examinations. A dan is a numbered black-belt-level grade; kendo uses the word even though kendo gear has no colored belt. Grades by examination run from first dan to eighth dan. Each higher exam requires a set number of years at the grade below.

The eighth dan examination is known in Japan as one of the hardest tests in any martial art. Candidates must have held seventh dan for many years. Very few pass in any year, and many try again and again. Panels of senior examiners judge the candidates' matches.

The grade system decides who may judge, teach and examine others, not who may enter a first match. A beginner can join a kendo club and compete in local events. In fencing, results and national rankings open doors; in kendo, examined grades carry much of the authority. Each sport answers the question of standing in its own way.

words.d: a numbered advanced grade in Japanese arts; kendo grants first to eighth dan by examination
a formal test before a panel that decides whether a person earns a grade
a person's recognized place in a sport, shown by results or grades

look.title: Two Kinds of Standing

look.prompt: What does each record measure, and why might each sport prefer its own kind?

check.why: The All Japan Kendo Federation runs the dan examinations.

check.why: Grades by examination run from first to eighth dan.

choices: Who may judge, teach and examine others

lessons.title: Wheelchair Fencing, Rome 1960
lessons.mainIdea: Wheelchair fencing was part of the first Paralympic Games in Rome in 1960, opening fencing's starting line to athletes with disabilities.
reading: In 1948 the doctor Ludwig Guttmann held a sports competition for injured military veterans at Stoke Mandeville Hospital in England. Many of them used wheelchairs after spinal injuries in the Second World War. Guttmann believed sport helped patients recover strength and confidence. His games grew each year.

In 1960 the event was held in Rome after the Olympic Games, and it is now counted as the first *Paralympic Games*. *Wheelchair fencing* was on its program. The wheelchairs are fixed to a frame on the floor, so fencers face each other at a set distance. Fencers use the same three weapons as in Olympic fencing.

Wheelchair fencing has been held at every Summer Paralympics since 1960. The rule of the fixed frame answered a practical question about who may start: it let athletes who use wheelchairs compete on equal terms. The event shows how a code can be rewritten to open a door, rather than keep one shut.

words.d: the international games for athletes with disabilities; the first counted Games were held in Rome in 1960
fencing in wheelchairs fixed to a floor frame; part of every Summer Paralympics since 1960
a doctor who began games for injured veterans at Stoke Mandeville, England, in 1948

check.why: Guttmann held his 1948 games at Stoke Mandeville Hospital in England.

check.why: The frame fixes the chairs at a set distance so athletes compete on equal terms.

check.why: Wheelchair fencing was part of the first Paralympic Games in Rome in 1960.

lessons.title: A Second Pair: Sumo and Schwingen
lessons.mainIdea: Japan's sumo and Switzerland's schwingen are both national wrestling traditions with their own bodies, rings and rules, so they can be compared by date.
reading: Professional sumo in Japan is run by the Japan Sumo Association. Its forerunner was formed in 1925 by joining the Tokyo and Osaka groups. Since 1958 it has held six grand tournaments a year. The association sets entry rules for new wrestlers, and since 2002 it has limited each training stable to one foreign-born wrestler.

*Schwingen* is Swiss wrestling, held in a ring covered with sawdust. Wrestlers wear short canvas trousers over their clothes. The Federal Wrestling Association, the Eidgenössischer Schwingerverband, was founded in 1895. Its biggest festival is held every three years, and the champion is traditionally given a bull as a prize.

The two can be compared with the same questions used for fencing and kendo. Sumo is professional; schwingen wrestlers are amateurs who win prizes in kind, such as livestock, not salaries. Sumo's home is a national arena; schwingen's is an outdoor festival. Each is a *national tradition*, and each body decides who may enter its ring.

words.d: Swiss wrestling held in a sawdust ring, organized by a federal association founded in 1895
in sumo, a training house where wrestlers live and practice under a stablemaster
a practice a country treats as part of its shared identity

lessons.title: Comparing Without a Winner
lessons.mainIdea: A strong comparison sets dated facts about origin, room, nation and code side by side and explains differences without ranking the arts.
reading: Historians of sport use *comparison* to see what is shared and what is particular. For fencing and kendo, the origin question has dated answers: the Paris charter of 1567 and the Edo halls of the early 1800s. The room question has answers too: the salle and the dojo. Each can be checked in records.

The nation question asks which states shaped each art. France gave fencing its words and its world body in 1913. Japan gave kendo its name, its national federation in 1952 and a place in school physical education. The code question asks who writes the rules: the FIE for fencing, the FIK and national federations for kendo.

A comparison becomes a *ranking* when it treats one set of answers as the standard. Calling kendo less modern because it uses flags, or fencing less serious because it uses a machine, adds a judgment the records do not support. The dated evidence shows two institutions that made different choices, each with its own reasons.

words.d: setting two things side by side to see what is shared and what is particular
ordering things from better to worse by one standard
records and facts that support a claim
